cards.front: Binary search on a sorted array — time and space?
cards.back: O(log n) time, O(1) space iteratively (O(log n) stack if recursive).

cards.front: Merge sort — time, space, stability?
cards.back: O(n log n) always, O(n) extra space, stable.

cards.front: Quicksort — average, worst, space?
cards.back: O(n log n) average, O(n²) worst on bad pivots, O(log n) stack. Not stable.

cards.front: Heap sort — time, space, stability?
cards.back: O(n log n) always, O(1) extra space, not stable.

cards.front: Building a heap from an unsorted array — cost?
cards.back: O(n), not O(n log n) — most nodes sift down only a level or two.

cards.front: Hash table lookup — average and worst case?
cards.back: O(1) average, O(n) worst when every key collides into one bucket.

cards.front: Appending to a dynamic array — amortized cost, and why?
cards.back: O(1) amortized: doubling makes n appends cost under 2n total work.

cards.front: BFS and DFS on a graph — time and space?
cards.back: O(V + E) time. BFS space is the widest level; DFS space is the deepest path.

cards.front: Dijkstra with a binary heap — time?
cards.back: O((V + E) log V). Fails on negative edge weights — use Bellman-Ford, O(V·E).

cards.front: Balanced BST — search, insert, delete?
cards.back: O(log n) each. Unbalanced degrades to O(n) on sorted insertions.

cards.front: Trie lookup of a word of length L?
cards.back: O(L), independent of how many words the trie holds.

cards.front: 0/1 knapsack DP — time and space?
cards.back: O(n·W) time, O(n·W) space, reducible to O(W) with a rolling row.

cards.front: Counting sort — time, and when is it usable?
cards.back: O(n + k) for k distinct keys — only when the key range is small and integral.

cards.front: Quickselect for the kth smallest — average and worst?
cards.back: O(n) average, O(n²) worst. Median-of-medians makes it O(n) worst-case.

cards.front: Which pattern: longest/shortest contiguous subarray meeting a condition?
cards.back: Sliding window — expand right, shrink left while the condition holds.

cards.front: Which pattern: a pair summing to a target in a sorted array, O(1) space?
cards.back: Two pointers from both ends — move left up when the sum is small, right down when large.

cards.front: Which pattern: detect a cycle in a linked list with O(1) space?
cards.back: Fast & slow pointers — they meet inside the cycle.

cards.front: Which pattern: overlapping intervals to merge or a room count?
cards.back: Merge intervals — sort by start, then merge or sweep the endpoints.

cards.front: Which pattern: k largest / k most frequent elements?
cards.back: Top-K with a size-k heap — O(n log k) instead of a full sort.

cards.front: Which pattern: many range-sum queries on a static array?
cards.back: Prefix sums — sum(l..r) = prefix[r+1] - prefix[l].

cards.front: Which pattern: minimise a maximum (capacity, speed, time) with a monotone feasibility check?
cards.back: Binary search on the answer, not on the array.

cards.front: Which pattern: next greater or previous smaller element?
cards.back: Monotonic stack — one pass, each element pushed and popped once.

cards.front: Which pattern: find missing/duplicate values in 1..n in O(1) space?
cards.back: Cyclic sort — swap each value to its index, then scan for the mismatch.

cards.front: Which pattern: merge k sorted lists?
cards.back: K-way merge with a size-k heap of the current heads — O(N log k).

cards.front: Which pattern: maximum non-overlapping activities?
cards.back: Greedy intervals — sort by end time and take the earliest finisher.

cards.front: Which pattern: generate all permutations, subsets or valid boards?
cards.back: Backtracking — choose, explore, un-choose, and prune early.

cards.front: Which pattern: tasks with prerequisites, or detect a cycle in a DAG?
cards.back: Topological sort — Kahn's in-degree queue or DFS post-order.

cards.front: Which pattern: connected components with dynamic merges?
cards.back: Union-Find with path compression and union by rank.

cards.front: Which pattern: count regions in a grid?
cards.back: Matrix traversal / flood fill — BFS or DFS from each unvisited cell.

cards.front: Which pattern: level-by-level tree output?
cards.back: Tree BFS — a queue, processing one full level per outer iteration.

cards.front: Which pattern: the median of a stream, updated after every insert?
cards.back: Two heaps — a max-heap of the smaller half, a min-heap of the larger, sizes within one.

cards.front: Which pattern: maximum of every fixed-width window in O(n)?
cards.back: Monotonic deque — evict expired indices at the front, pop dominated ones at the back.

cards.front: Which pattern: pick a subset of items maximising value under a capacity?
cards.back: 0/1 knapsack DP — dp[c] = max(dp[c], v + dp[c - w]), capacity descending.

cards.front: Which pattern: compare two sequences position by position?
cards.back: Grid DP — dp[i][j] over the two prefixes; diagonal on a match, best neighbour otherwise.

cards.front: Which pattern: range sums with updates interleaved between the queries?
cards.back: Fenwick or segment tree — both O(log n); prefix sums would rebuild on every write.

cards.front: Which pattern: autocomplete or matching a whole dictionary at once?
cards.back: Trie — O(L) in the key length, independent of dictionary size, and prunes the search.

cards.front: Which pattern: distance from every cell to its nearest of many sources?
cards.back: Multi-source BFS — seed all sources at distance 0, then run one ordinary BFS.

cards.front: Which pattern: cheapest route when edges carry non-negative weights?
cards.back: Dijkstra with a min-heap. Any negative edge forces Bellman-Ford instead.

cards.front: Which pattern: maximum overlapping intervals, or many range updates read once?
cards.back: Line sweep with ±1 endpoint events, or a difference array plus one prefix sum.

cards.front: Which pattern: best contiguous subarray with no window size given?
cards.back: Kadane — cur = max(a[i], cur + a[i]), tracking the global best each step.

cards.front: Which pattern: compare every length-m substring of a long string?
cards.back: Rolling hash — O(1) per slide, then verify hits because hashes collide.

cards.front: Which pattern: count subarrays summing to k in one pass?
cards.back: Prefix sum plus a hash map of counts, seeded {0: 1}.

cards.front: Which pattern: first element ≥ x, or a target in a rotated sorted array?
cards.back: Modified binary search — hunt the boundary; in a rotation, one half is always sorted.

cards.front: Which pattern: a correct exponential recursion that repeats subproblems?
cards.back: Top-down memoization — cache by the argument tuple; cost = states × work per state.

cards.front: Which pattern: stock buy/sell with cooldowns, or no two adjacent picks?
cards.back: State machine DP — one scalar per mode, updated from the previous index's values.

cards.front: Which pattern: assignment or TSP with n ≤ 20?
cards.back: Bitmask DP — the mask is the set of used items; O(2^n · n).

cards.front: Which pattern: count inversions in an array?
cards.back: Divide and conquer — merge sort, counting the cross-boundary pairs during the merge.

cards.front: Which pattern: rotate a matrix 90° in place?
cards.back: Transpose, then reverse each row. (r, c) → (c, n-1-r).

cards.front: Which pattern: split people into two non-conflicting groups?
cards.back: Two-colouring — bipartite iff no odd cycle; BFS/DFS every component.

cards.front: Which pattern: insert, delete and getRandom all in O(1)?
cards.back: Paired structures — hash map of value → index plus a dense array, swap-and-pop on delete.

cards.front: Which pattern: evaluate a nested encoded string or expression?
cards.back: Stack of contexts — push the enclosing state on open, fold the child in on close.

cards.front: Which pattern: subset-sum flavoured question with n around 40?
cards.back: Meet in the middle — enumerate both halves, sort one, binary-search the join. O(2^(n/2)).

cards.front: Which pattern: uniform sample from a stream of unknown length?
cards.back: Reservoir sampling — keep k, replace with probability k/i as the i-th item arrives.

cards.front: Which pattern: find the shortest repeating block of a string?
cards.back: Prefix function — period is n - pi[n-1], valid only when it divides n.

cards.front: Which pattern: merging or bursting elements where neighbours change the cost?
cards.back: Interval DP — dp[i][j] over ranges, filled shortest-length first, enumerating what acts last.

cards.front: Which pattern: best value over a tree where a node depends on its subtrees?
cards.back: Tree DP — post-order; return one downward branch to the parent, combine both locally.

cards.front: Which pattern: many k-th ancestor or LCA queries on a static tree?
cards.back: Binary lifting — up[j][v] = up[j-1][up[j-1][v]], O(n log n) build, O(log n) query.

cards.front: Which pattern: sort into three categories in place, one pass?
cards.back: Dutch national flag — low/mid/high; after swapping from high, do not advance mid.

cards.front: How do you justify a greedy algorithm?
cards.back: Exchange argument — rewrite any optimal solution to start with the greedy choice without loss, then induct.

cards.front: Which pattern: longest palindromic substring in O(1) space?
cards.back: Expand around centre — 2n-1 centres, both odd and even parities.

cards.front: Which pattern: k-th smallest key in a BST?
cards.back: Iterative in-order with a stack — sorted order, stop after k pops.

cards.front: Which pattern: longest increasing subsequence in O(n log n)?
cards.back: Tails array — binary-search the first tail ≥ x and replace it; length is len(tails).

cards.front: Which pattern: maximum XOR of a pair, with n too big for O(n²)?
cards.back: Bit trie — insert MSB first, then walk the opposite bit at every level.

cards.front: Which pattern: longest path or path count over prerequisites?
cards.back: DAG DP — relax edges forward in topological order; longest path is only easy because it is acyclic.

cards.front: Which pattern: a game where both players play optimally?
cards.back: Game theory DP — best(s) = max over moves of (gain − best(s')); negate across the turn.

cards.front: Which pattern: minimum rooms, or tasks with a cooldown?
cards.back: Sort by arrival, min-heap of end times; heap size is the concurrency.

cards.front: Which pattern: many submatrix sum queries on a static grid?
cards.back: 2D prefix sums — big − above − left + corner, on a zero-padded table.

cards.front: Array vs linked list — the real trade-off?
cards.back: Array: O(1) random access, O(n) middle insert. Linked list: O(1) splice given the node, no random access, worse cache locality.

cards.front: When does a hash map beat a balanced BST?
cards.back: When you need only point lookups. A BST wins when you need ordering: range queries, successor, sorted iteration.

cards.front: What does a heap give you that a sorted array does not?
cards.back: O(log n) insert with O(1) access to the min/max, without maintaining full order.

cards.front: When is a deque the right structure?
cards.back: Push/pop at both ends in O(1) — sliding-window maxima, BFS with 0/1 weights.

cards.front: What problem does a Fenwick (BIT) tree solve?
cards.back: Prefix sums with point updates, both O(log n), in far less code and space than a segment tree.

cards.front: Segment tree vs Fenwick tree?
cards.back: Segment tree handles any associative range query (min, max, gcd) and range updates with lazy propagation; Fenwick is smaller but essentially sum-only.

cards.front: What is a Bloom filter's guarantee?
cards.back: No false negatives, some false positives, and no deletions — a cheap membership pre-filter.

cards.front: How does an LRU cache reach O(1) for get and put?
cards.back: Hash map to nodes plus a doubly linked list for recency; both ends splice in constant time.

cards.front: Why does a BST degrade to O(n)?
cards.back: Sorted insertions make it a linked list. AVL / red-black rotations keep the height O(log n).

cards.front: What is a disjoint-set union used for?
cards.back: Connectivity and grouping — Kruskal's MST, cycle detection in an undirected graph, dynamic components.

cards.front: Adjacency list vs adjacency matrix?
cards.back: List: O(V + E) space, best for sparse graphs. Matrix: O(V²) space, O(1) edge lookup, fine for dense graphs.

cards.front: Stack vs queue in traversal?
cards.back: Stack (or recursion) gives DFS; queue gives BFS, which finds the fewest-edge path in an unweighted graph.

cards.front: Precision vs recall — in one line each?
cards.back: Precision: of what I flagged, how much was right. Recall: of what was actually positive, how much I caught.

cards.front: When is accuracy a misleading metric?
cards.back: Under class imbalance — 99.5% accuracy is what predicting the majority class alone scores.

cards.front: What does F1 balance, and when is PR-AUC preferred over ROC-AUC?
cards.back: F1 is the harmonic mean of precision and recall. PR-AUC is more informative when positives are rare.

cards.front: High bias vs high variance — the symptom?
cards.back: High bias: poor on train and test (underfit). High variance: great on train, poor on test (overfit).

cards.front: L1 vs L2 regularisation?
cards.back: L1 drives weights to exactly zero and selects features; L2 shrinks weights smoothly and handles correlated features better.

cards.front: Why standardise features before PCA or k-means?
cards.back: Both use Euclidean distance/variance, so a large-unit feature would dominate purely because of its scale.

cards.front: What is data leakage, and its most common cause?
cards.back: Information unavailable at prediction time entering training — usually fitting a transform or splitting after aggregation.

cards.front: Bagging vs boosting?
cards.back: Bagging trains independent models in parallel to cut variance; boosting trains sequentially on prior errors to cut bias.

cards.front: Why does the vanishing gradient problem happen, and one fix?
cards.back: Repeated multiplication by small derivatives through depth. Fixes: ReLU, residual connections, normalisation, LSTM gates.

cards.front: What does dropout do at training and at inference?
cards.back: Randomly zeroes units during training to prevent co-adaptation; at inference it is off, with activations scaled to match.

cards.front: Self-attention cost in sequence length n?
cards.back: O(n²·d) time and O(n²) memory — the reason long-context work targets exactly this term.

cards.front: Why do transformers need positional encodings?
cards.back: Self-attention is permutation-invariant; without position information the model cannot tell word order.

cards.front: Batch norm vs layer norm — when each?
cards.back: Batch norm normalises across the batch (vision, large batches); layer norm across features per example (transformers, variable-length sequences).

cards.front: Value-based vs policy-based RL?
cards.back: Value-based (Q-learning, DQN) learns action values and acts greedily; policy-based (REINFORCE, PPO) optimises the policy directly and handles continuous actions.

cards.front: On-policy vs off-policy?
cards.back: On-policy learns from the current policy's data (SARSA, PPO); off-policy learns from other data, enabling replay buffers (Q-learning, DQN).

cards.front: CAP theorem in one sentence?
cards.back: Under a network partition you keep either consistency or availability — partitions are not optional, so pick CP or AP and say why.

cards.front: What is the hard part of caching?
cards.back: Invalidation. Decide TTL vs write-through up front, and name the staleness the design accepts.

cards.front: Why consistent hashing instead of hash mod N?
cards.back: Adding or removing a node remaps only ~1/N of keys instead of nearly all of them.

cards.front: What does a message queue buy you?
cards.back: Decoupling and buffering — producers survive slow consumers, and spikes are absorbed instead of dropped.

cards.front: Read replicas: what do you give up?
cards.back: Freshness. Followers lag the leader, so reads can be stale — fine for feeds, not for read-after-write.

cards.front: How do you pick a shard key?
cards.back: Even load distribution and locality for the dominant query. A monotonic key (timestamp, auto-id) creates a hot shard.

cards.front: Two common rate-limiting algorithms?
cards.back: Token bucket (allows bursts up to the bucket size) and sliding window (smoother, more state).

cards.front: What does idempotency give an API?
cards.back: Safe retries — a repeated request has the same effect as one, which is what makes at-least-once delivery workable.

cards.front: First step of any design round?
cards.back: Clarify functional requirements and non-functional targets (scale, latency, availability), then estimate QPS and storage before drawing.

cards.front: When is SQL the wrong default?
cards.back: When the access pattern is a huge single-key keyspace with no joins and write throughput exceeding one primary — but say what consistency you are trading away.

cards.front: What is the point of a CDN?
cards.back: Serving static and media content from an edge near the user — lower latency, and origin bandwidth offloaded.

cards.front: Training/serving skew — what is it and why does it matter?
cards.back: Features computed differently offline and online; it is the usual reason a strong offline model underperforms live.

cards.front: Why two-stage retrieval and ranking?
cards.back: Scoring millions of candidates per request is infeasible — a cheap retriever narrows to hundreds, then an expensive ranker orders them.

cards.front: How do you roll out a new model safely?
cards.back: Shadow traffic first, then an A/B test on the online metric, then a ramp — with versioned artifacts so rollback is one step.
